18	The Defendants contend that the Complaint should be dismissed in its entirety for failure to comply with the 2004 Agreement’s dispute resolution and mediation clause. L.P./Inc. Mot. to Dismiss at 12-13. The clause provides that “[a]ny dispute, controversy or claim arising out of or relating to this Agreement, or the breach, termination, or invalidity thereof shall first be referred by the parties to their senior-level executives for attempted resolution through good-faith negotiations.” Compl. Ex. A § 9.1 (emphasis added). Should negotiations fail, thirty days after making a written request to initiate those negotiations, “either Party may, by written notice to the other, require that the Dispute be referred to non-binding mediation administered by the American Arbitration Association.” Id. (emphasis added). The Defendants assert that Skold did not refer a dispute to a senior-level executive for negotiations and failed to make a written request that the dispute be referred to nonbinding mediation. L.P./Inc. Mot. to Dismiss at 12-13. Skold responds that the language of the mediation clause is permissive (“either Party may ... require”) and also argues that, in any event, Inc. has waived its right to invoke the clause because it participated in litigation over the dispute in the cancellation action before the TTAB. See Pl.’s L.P./Inc. Opp’n at 14-15.
19	The dispute resolution clause in the 2004 Agreement contains two clauses, one of which is mandatory (the parties shall refer the matter to senior executives to attempt to negotiate a resolution) and the other which is permissive (the parties may refer the matter to nonbinding mediation). Given the voluntary nature of the latter, this Court agrees with Skold that he was not required to refer this dispute to mediation before bringing suit here against Inc.
20	L.P. and S.A., who are not parties to the 2004 Agreement, also contend that the dispute resolution clause requires their dismissal from this action. In essence, they urge this Court to accept the contention that a nonparty to an agreement should be permitted to force a signatory party to engage in negotiations pursuant to a permissive mediation clause in that agreement as a condition precedent to filing suit but cite no relevant case or statute in support of this contention. See United States v. Benish, 5 F.3d 20, 26 (3d Cir.1993) (rejecting a party’s claim where the party “provided] no legal support for his argument or any persuasive reason” for the court to find in his favor). The Court sees no persuasive reason to dismiss Skold’s entire Complaint based on this unsupported argument. Accordingly, the motion to dismiss the Complaint against L.P. and S.A. on this ground shall be denied.
21	Regarding Inc.: although Skold did fail to bring in a senior-level executive to try to resolve the dispute — as he was required to do under the dispute resolution provision — Inc.’s participation in the TTAB proceedings waived any rights it may have had to seek to have the parties’ executives negotiate an end to the dispute. See, e.g., LBL Skysystems (USA), Inc. v. APG-Am., Inc., No. 02-5379, 2005 WL 2140240, at *30 (E.D.Pa. Aug. 31, 2005) (holding that a “party that engages in discovery and files pretrial motions waives a contract’s alternative dispute resolution provision”); Smith v. IMG Worldwide, Inc., 360 F.Supp.2d 681, 687 (E.D.Pa.2005) (finding that a party’s engaging in motion practice and providing “substantial discovery” constituted waiver of contractual alternative dispute resolution provision).
22	Viewing the four years’ worth of docket entries in the TTAB action, the Court considers that Inc. did not file a motion to stay the TTAB proceedings pending executive-level negotiations and instead filed, inter alia, motions to dismiss, a protective order, multiple summary judgment motions (one of which was partially granted in its favor), and a final brief in preparation for trial. See, e.g., Sköld v. Galderma Labs., Inc., Cancellation No. 92052897, 2012 WL 5902083 (T.T.A.B. Nov. 8, 2012) (granting Inc.’s motion for partial summary judgment on Skold’s abandonment claim). See also generally Registrant’s Trial Brief, Sköld v. Galderma Labs., Inc., Cancellation No. 92052897 (T.T.A.B. Aug. 13, 2014), Docket No. 81. This four-year history of litigation in the cancellation action — from filing nearly through trial — is, on its face, inconsistent with the notion that Inc. was willing to engage in the good-faith executive-level negotiations required by the dispute resolution provision.
23	Moreover, the Court can look to the TTAB’s grant of partial summary judgment in favor of Inc. and dismissing Skold’s abandonment claim as a concrete example of an instance where Inc.’s conduct inconsistent with the dispute resolution clause caused prejudice to Skold, not to mention the expenditure of time, cost, and resources attendant to maintaining a multi-year trademark cancellation action. The Defendants have undisputedly accepted the judicial process and have demonstrated that fact by: (1) Inc.’s failure to raise the issue of good-faith negotiations promptly before the TTAB; (2) Inc.’s engaging in discovery in the TTAB action; (3) Inc.’s filing of several pretrial motions in the TTAB action, none of which raise the issue of negotiation; and (4) the Defendants’ decision to wait until the case was ready to proceed to trial before the TTAB and until a Complaint was filed in this Court before asserting Skold’s failure to negotiate as grounds for a motion to dismiss. See St. Clair Area Sch. Dist. Bd. of Educ. v. E.I. Assocs., 733 A.2d 677, 682 n. 6 (Pa.Commw.Ct.1999) (“The key to determining whether [an alternative dispute resolution procedure] has been waived is whether the party, by virtue of its conduct, has accepted the judicial process.”). Inc. cannot now attempt to stand on the alternative dispute resolution clause as a reason for dismissal. Its right to invoke the clause has been waived.
24	```

1	# Worked example — Category 1.3 — general-vs-specific / list scope
2	
3	Contract `93FSupp3d375_personal_deposit_account_agreement`, filed in 93 F.Supp.3d 375. The full text is in `contract.txt` beside this file.
4	
5	A court construed **4** of this contract's provisions; the other **251** it did not. Read that as the base rate to expect, NOT as a quota to reproduce.
6	
7	## HIGH RISK — a federal court construed this provision
8	
9	"Part I — International ACH and Wire Transactions (NACHA Operating Rules)"  (risk type: 1.3)
10	
11	```
12	International ACH and Wire Transactions If your Account receives incoming ACH transactions (either credits or debits) or wire transfers initiated from outside of the United States, both you and we are subject to the Operating Rules and Guidelines of the National Automated Clearing House Association (“NACHA”) or the rules of any wire transfer system involved, and the laws enforced by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (“OFAC”). Under such rules and laws, we may temporarily suspend processing of a transaction for greater scrutiny or verification against the OFAC list of blocked parties, which may result in delayed settlement, posting and/or availability of funds. If we determine there is a violation, or if we cannot satisfactorily resolve a suspected or potential violation, the subject funds will be blocked as required by law. If you believe you have adequate grounds to seek the return of any blocked funds, it is your sole responsibility to pursue the matter with the appropriate governmental authorities. Please see the OFAC website for procedures and form required to seek a release of blocked funds.
13	```
14	
15	### What the court said, verbatim from the opinion in 93 F.Supp.3d 375
16	
17	```
18	The bulk of Plaintiffs’ breach claim centers around their argument that TD’s conduct violated the NACHA Rules, which Plaintiffs claim were incorporated into the Account Agreement. See Compl. at ¶ 166-67. In order to address this claim we must first determine whether the NACHA rules were in fact incorporated. In support of this point, Plaintiffs cite to page 16 of the Account Agreement, which states in relevant part:
19	International ACH and Wire Transactions
20	If your Account receives incoming ACH transactions (either credits or debits) or wire transfers initiated from outside of the United States, both you and we are subject to the Operating Rules and Guidelines of the National Automated Clearing House Association (“NACHA”) or the rules of any wire transfer system involved....
21	As TD points out, this provision does not refer to all ACH transactions, but rather only to those initiated from outside of the United States. Motion to Dismiss at 18 (Doc. No. 23). Taking the Plaintiffs’ allegations as true, the Complaint raises a plausible claim that some number of the loans originated outside of the United States. 191	I. Executive Summary
192	
193	MORTGAGE FUND °08 LLC (the “Company”), sponsored by the principals of R.E. Loans, LLC, offers a
194	new and attractive opportunity for qualified investors to achieve superior returns with a conservative risk
195	profile through the purchase of promissory notes (the “Notes”) issued by the Company. The Company is
196	targeting to return approximately 8.00% or more per year on the Noteholders investments. The Notes will
197	be secured by the assets of the Company.
198	
199	The Company will be formed as a Delaware limited liability company for the purpose of lending capital
200	raised by the sale of Notes to borrowers (the “Portfolio Borrowers”) to finance the ownership,
201	entitlement, development or rehabilitation of commercial real estate or for other real estate related
202	purposes throughout the United States (the “Portfolic Loans”), The Portfolio Loans will be secured by
203	liens against real property and associated personal property.
204	
205	The Company will be managed by its manager, The Mortgage Fund LLC, a California limited liability
206	company formed for this purpose (the “Manager” or “The Mortgage Fund LLC’). The Manager is
207	owned and led by Walter Ng and Kelly Ng (the “Managing Directors” or “Principals”), who together
208	bring to the Company more than 81 years of experience in mortgage lending and investing among them.
209	The Manager expects to hire Bar-K, Inc. to provide Portfolio Loan origination, brokerage and
210	administration services to the Company (“Loan Services”) as “Servicer”, comparable to the services that
211	Bar-K, Inc. provides to R.E. Loans, LLC and that it provided to its predecessor investment funds. Bar-K
212	Inc, is managed by Barney Ng, and owned by Bamey and Kelly Ng. Walter Ng, Kelly Ng and Barney Ng
213	also manage and own, with Bruce Horwitz, M.D., B-4 Partners, LLC, the sponsor of R.E. Loans LLC,
214	and were sponsors of prior investment funds to R.E. Loans, LLC.
215	
216	In order to participate in this opportunity, each prospective investor will subscribe to purchase Notes
217	pursuant to a Note Purchase Agreement with the Company by “loaning” their investment capital to the
218	Company (their “Loan Amounts”). Notes will be issued to investors whose subscriptions are accepted by
219	the Company (“Nofeholders”), in its discretion, at the next closing held by the Company, The initial
220	closing is expected to be on or before December 3, 2007, and the Company expects to hold closings on
221	the first day of each calendar month thereafter through May 1, 2009, although there is no assurance that
222	there will be a subsequent closing or that a closing will be held each month, The Company has not
223	targeted a minimum or maximum amount of capital to be raised by a sale of Notes. The Manager, the
224	Principals, their family members, and their affiliates may also purchase Notes on the same terms as the
225	Notes purchased by investors.
226	
227	The Notes will bear simple interest at a rate determined quarterly by the Managing Directors, subject to a
228	minimum average rate of eight percent (8%) annualized, The Notes will be secured by the assets of the
229	Company. Regardless of when purchased, each Note will have a term ending December 31, 2014,
230	subject, in the discretion of the Company, to a six month extension that would be applicable to all
231	outstanding Notes. Interest will be payable quarterly, but payment of principal will be deferred, at the
232	discretion of the Company, until the maturity of the Note, although principal may be prepaid at any time
233	without penalty.
234	
235	The Notes are an illiquid and long-term investment. No investor should subscribe to purchase a Note
236	unless it is prepared to hold the Note until its maturity. Although the Company may, in its discretion,
237	prepay a Note at any time, a Noteholder may not request prepayment of a Note until it has held the Note
238	for a minimum of one year from the date of its issue, and the granting of such request is within the sole
239	discretion of the Company. The Notes will not be transferable except under very limited circumstances
240	and then only in the discretion of the Manager. There is no secondary market for sale of the Notes and
241	none is expected to develop.

269	II. Private Mortgage Lending
270	
271	The Company intends to invest in conservatively underwritten real estate mortgage loans with borrowers
272	who are experienced in real estate operations and finance by directly controlling the sourcing, funding and
273	administration of such loans based upon criteria the Principals have found to be successful in the past.
274	The Company will not operate in the sub-prime mortgage market and will not source loans for the
275	purpose of resale. Instead, it will focus the portfolio on loans secured by quality real estate for generation
276	of income to the Company.
277	
278	Lending Market Opportunities
279	
280	There is a substantial demand for private capital that can be funded on a timely basis. The Managers
281	believe this is true in a rising or falling real estate market.
282	
283	Investor Opportunities
284	
285	To date, the Principais and their affiliates have a proven lending record of sponsoring investments in well-
286	diversified performing loans that produce solid returns to their investors. To date, no investor has
287	experienced a loss of investment principal through investment vehicles sponsored by the Principals or
288	their affiliates. Although there is no assurance that investors in the Company will experience similar
289	results, the Manager believes that the past real estate lending success of the Principals and their affiliates
290	will generate comparable opportunities for the Company and its Noteholders.
291	
292	RE. Loans
293	
294	The Principals and their affiliates, through B-4+ Partners, are currently sponsoring and managing R.E.
295	Loans, LLC, a private real estate lender. As of the date of this Memorandum, R.E. Loans has a portfolio
296	of over 60 secured mortgage loans in diverse markets with aggregate principal capital of $750 million.
297	Over its lifetime, R.E. Loans has made 325 mortgage loans with an aggregate principal of $1.5 billion and
298	generated returns for investors averaging 8.5% per annum.
299	
300	Prior Limited Partnerships
301	
302	R.E, Loans was formed in 2002 as a new investment fund by a merger of nine limited partnerships
303	sponsored and managed by predecessors to B-4 Partners. These nine limited partnerships were
304	responsible for more than 500 mortgage loans with aggregate principal of approximately $150 million.
305	Prior to the merger, these partnerships had diverse portfolios averaging greater than 8% return to investors
306	per annum, on a weighted basis.
307

309	
310	Bar-K, Inc, the Company’s Servicer, brings to the Company 33 years of experience in the origination,
311	management, work-out and collection of real estate mortgage loans. To date, Bar-K, Inc. has a 100%
312	collection record with respect to loans it administers. This experience has contributed greatly to the
313	success of R.E. Loans and its nine predecessor limited partnership, none of which experienced a loss of
314	principal or interest with respect to their mortgage loan portfolio.

538	obligation to the Noteholders nor, at the time of this offering, does it have a fiduciary obligation to the
539	Company’s members or contractual obligation under the Operating Agreement independent of its own
540	interests in the Company.

549	faith or willful misconduct. The Operating Agreement also provides that the Company shall indemnify
550	the Manager and Servicer against liability and related expenses (including reasonable attorneys’ fees and
551	costs) incurred in dealing with the Company, Noteholders or third parties, so long as no fraud, bad faith or
552	willful misconduct on the part of the Manager or Servicer is involved. A successful indemnification of
553	the Manager or Servicer or any litigation that may arise in connection with their indemnification could
554	deplete the assets of the Company, thereby reducing the assets available to pay the Notes. Therefore,

556	provisions in the Operating Agreement.

749	IV. Portfolio Loan Criteria and Policies

751	General Standards for Mortgage Loans
752	
753	The Company will engage in the business of making loans secured by deeds of trust that encumber real
754	estate located primarily in the United States, its territories and possessions. The Company may also
755	invest indirectly in a loan by acquiring an ownership interest in an entity formed for the sole purpose of
756	holding a qualifying loan. To the extent the Manager believes it to be in the best interests of the
757	Company, the Company may also make or invest in construction loans for the purpose of constructing
758	various types of residential and/or commercial properties, which construction loans would be secured by
759	such properties. The Company may also make occasional loans to individuals and entities collateralized
760	by loans that are secured by deeds of trust. The Company’s loans will not be insured or guaranteed by
761	any governmental agency or private entity.
762	
763	The Company expects to select loans for investment pursuant to a strict set of guidelines set forth below,
764	which guidelines are designed to set standards for the quality of the real property security given for the
765	loans.
766	
767	‘Type of Property/Loan Loan to Value Ratio
768	
769	Improved Property (whether residential, commercial or industrial) 70%

772	Priority of Mortgages

774	Most Company loans are expected to be secured by a first deed of trust on the real property (the “Security
775	Property”) which is to be used as security for the loan. The Company’s investment in loans that are
776	secured by a junior deed of trust will not exceed twenty percent (20%) of the Company’s entire Loan
777	Portfolio.

779	Geographic Area of Lending Activity
780	
781	The Company will limit its lending activity primarily to deeds of trust on properties located in the United
782	States, its territories and possessions (“U.S. Praperties”), but may invest up to 20% of total Company
783	Capital in loans secured by non-U.S. Properties if the loan meets the Company’s lending criteria.
784	
785	Loan-to-Value Ratios
786	
787	The amount of the Company’s loan combined with the outstanding debt secured by any senior deed of
788	trust on the security property generally will not exceed the percentages stated above, based a valuation of
789	the security property as determined by either the Manager or an independent written appraisal. Appraisals
790	and loan-to-value ratios may be determined on an as-completed basis with respect to construction or
791	home improvement loans, however, loan funds may be withheld to be paid out upon inspection as
792	improvements are made.
793	
794	Finally, the foregoing loan-to-value ratio will not apply to purchase-money financing offered by the
795	Company to sell any real estate owned (acquired through foreclosure) or to refinance an existing loan that
796	is in default at the time of maturity. In such cases, the Manager shall be free to accept any reasonable
797	financing terms that it deems to be in the best interests of the Company, in its sole discretion. No such

849	purchases loans, the Company shall receive assignments of all beneficial interest in any documents

I. Executive Summary

MORTGAGE FUND °08 LLC (the “Company”), sponsored by the principals of R.E. Loans, LLC, offers a
new and attractive opportunity for qualified investors to achieve superior returns with a conservative risk
profile through the purchase of promissory notes (the “Notes”) issued by the Company. The Company is
targeting to return approximately 8.00% or more per year on the Noteholders investments. The Notes will
be secured by the assets of the Company.

The Company will be formed as a Delaware limited liability company for the purpose of lending capital
raised by the sale of Notes to borrowers (the “Portfolio Borrowers”) to finance the ownership,
entitlement, development or rehabilitation of commercial real estate or for other real estate related
purposes throughout the United States (the “Portfolic Loans”), The Portfolio Loans will be secured by
liens against real property and associated personal property.

The Company will be managed by its manager, The Mortgage Fund LLC, a California limited liability
company formed for this purpose (the “Manager” or “The Mortgage Fund LLC’). The Manager is
owned and led by Walter Ng and Kelly Ng (the “Managing Directors” or “Principals”), who together
bring to the Company more than 81 years of experience in mortgage lending and investing among them.
The Manager expects to hire Bar-K, Inc. to provide Portfolio Loan origination, brokerage and
administration services to the Company (“Loan Services”) as “Servicer”, comparable to the services that
Bar-K, Inc. provides to R.E. Loans, LLC and that it provided to its predecessor investment funds. Bar-K
Inc, is managed by Barney Ng, and owned by Bamey and Kelly Ng. Walter Ng, Kelly Ng and Barney Ng
also manage and own, with Bruce Horwitz, M.D., B-4 Partners, LLC, the sponsor of R.E. Loans LLC,
and were sponsors of prior investment funds to R.E. Loans, LLC.

In order to participate in this opportunity, each prospective investor will subscribe to purchase Notes
pursuant to a Note Purchase Agreement with the Company by “loaning” their investment capital to the
Company (their “Loan Amounts”). Notes will be issued to investors whose subscriptions are accepted by
the Company (“Nofeholders”), in its discretion, at the next closing held by the Company, The initial
closing is expected to be on or before December 3, 2007, and the Company expects to hold closings on
the first day of each calendar month thereafter through May 1, 2009, although there is no assurance that
there will be a subsequent closing or that a closing will be held each month, The Company has not
targeted a minimum or maximum amount of capital to be raised by a sale of Notes. The Manager, the
Principals, their family members, and their affiliates may also purchase Notes on the same terms as the
Notes purchased by investors.

The Notes will bear simple interest at a rate determined quarterly by the Managing Directors, subject to a
minimum average rate of eight percent (8%) annualized, The Notes will be secured by the assets of the
Company. Regardless of when purchased, each Note will have a term ending December 31, 2014,
subject, in the discretion of the Company, to a six month extension that would be applicable to all
outstanding Notes. Interest will be payable quarterly, but payment of principal will be deferred, at the
discretion of the Company, until the maturity of the Note, although principal may be prepaid at any time
without penalty.

The Notes are an illiquid and long-term investment. No investor should subscribe to purchase a Note
unless it is prepared to hold the Note until its maturity. Although the Company may, in its discretion,
prepay a Note at any time, a Noteholder may not request prepayment of a Note until it has held the Note
for a minimum of one year from the date of its issue, and the granting of such request is within the sole
discretion of the Company. The Notes will not be transferable except under very limited circumstances
and then only in the discretion of the Manager. There is no secondary market for sale of the Notes and
none is expected to develop.

II. Private Mortgage Lending

The Company intends to invest in conservatively underwritten real estate mortgage loans with borrowers
who are experienced in real estate operations and finance by directly controlling the sourcing, funding and
administration of such loans based upon criteria the Principals have found to be successful in the past.
The Company will not operate in the sub-prime mortgage market and will not source loans for the
purpose of resale. Instead, it will focus the portfolio on loans secured by quality real estate for generation
of income to the Company.

Lending Market Opportunities

There is a substantial demand for private capital that can be funded on a timely basis. The Managers
believe this is true in a rising or falling real estate market.

Investor Opportunities

To date, the Principais and their affiliates have a proven lending record of sponsoring investments in well-
diversified performing loans that produce solid returns to their investors. To date, no investor has
experienced a loss of investment principal through investment vehicles sponsored by the Principals or
their affiliates. Although there is no assurance that investors in the Company will experience similar
results, the Manager believes that the past real estate lending success of the Principals and their affiliates
will generate comparable opportunities for the Company and its Noteholders.

RE. Loans

The Principals and their affiliates, through B-4+ Partners, are currently sponsoring and managing R.E.
Loans, LLC, a private real estate lender. As of the date of this Memorandum, R.E. Loans has a portfolio
of over 60 secured mortgage loans in diverse markets with aggregate principal capital of $750 million.
Over its lifetime, R.E. Loans has made 325 mortgage loans with an aggregate principal of $1.5 billion and
generated returns for investors averaging 8.5% per annum.

Prior Limited Partnerships

R.E, Loans was formed in 2002 as a new investment fund by a merger of nine limited partnerships
sponsored and managed by predecessors to B-4 Partners. These nine limited partnerships were
responsible for more than 500 mortgage loans with aggregate principal of approximately $150 million.
Prior to the merger, these partnerships had diverse portfolios averaging greater than 8% return to investors
per annum, on a weighted basis.

Mortgage Servicing and Administration: Bar-K, Inc.

Bar-K, Inc, the Company’s Servicer, brings to the Company 33 years of experience in the origination,
management, work-out and collection of real estate mortgage loans. To date, Bar-K, Inc. has a 100%
collection record with respect to loans it administers. This experience has contributed greatly to the
success of R.E. Loans and its nine predecessor limited partnership, none of which experienced a loss of
principal or interest with respect to their mortgage loan portfolio.

IV. Portfolio Loan Criteria and Policies

General Standards for Mortgage Loans

The Company will engage in the business of making loans secured by deeds of trust that encumber real
estate located primarily in the United States, its territories and possessions. The Company may also
invest indirectly in a loan by acquiring an ownership interest in an entity formed for the sole purpose of
holding a qualifying loan. To the extent the Manager believes it to be in the best interests of the
Company, the Company may also make or invest in construction loans for the purpose of constructing
various types of residential and/or commercial properties, which construction loans would be secured by
such properties. The Company may also make occasional loans to individuals and entities collateralized
by loans that are secured by deeds of trust. The Company’s loans will not be insured or guaranteed by
any governmental agency or private entity.

The Company expects to select loans for investment pursuant to a strict set of guidelines set forth below,
which guidelines are designed to set standards for the quality of the real property security given for the
loans.

‘Type of Property/Loan Loan to Value Ratio

Improved Property (whether residential, commercial or industrial) 70%

Land 50%
Priority of Mortgages

Most Company loans are expected to be secured by a first deed of trust on the real property (the “Security
Property”) which is to be used as security for the loan. The Company’s investment in loans that are
secured by a junior deed of trust will not exceed twenty percent (20%) of the Company’s entire Loan
Portfolio.

Geographic Area of Lending Activity

The Company will limit its lending activity primarily to deeds of trust on properties located in the United
States, its territories and possessions (“U.S. Praperties”), but may invest up to 20% of total Company
Capital in loans secured by non-U.S. Properties if the loan meets the Company’s lending criteria.

Loan-to-Value Ratios

The amount of the Company’s loan combined with the outstanding debt secured by any senior deed of
trust on the security property generally will not exceed the percentages stated above, based a valuation of
the security property as determined by either the Manager or an independent written appraisal. Appraisals
and loan-to-value ratios may be determined on an as-completed basis with respect to construction or
home improvement loans, however, loan funds may be withheld to be paid out upon inspection as
improvements are made.

Finally, the foregoing loan-to-value ratio will not apply to purchase-money financing offered by the
Company to sell any real estate owned (acquired through foreclosure) or to refinance an existing loan that
is in default at the time of maturity. In such cases, the Manager shall be free to accept any reasonable
financing terms that it deems to be in the best interests of the Company, in its sole discretion. No such

The term of Company loans will vary at the discretion of the Manager. Company loans will generally

amount of the loan will be partially or fully repaid in equal monthly installments of principal and interest
over the term), or may provide for monthly payments of interest only during the term with a “balloon
payment” due at the end of the term.

Credit Evaluations

The Manager may consider the income level and general creditworthiness of a borrower, and any
guarantor, to determine a borrower’s ability to repay the Company loan according to its terms, but such
considerations are subordinate to a determination that a borrower has sufficient equity in the security
property to satisfy the loan-to-value ratios described above. Therefore, the Company may make loans to
borrowers who are in default under other of their obligations (e.g., to consolidate their debts) or who do
not have sources of income that would be sufficient to qualify for loans from other lenders such as banks
or savings and loan associations.

Escrow Conditions

Company loans will be funded through an escrow account handled by the Manager or a qualified title
insurance or escrow company, The escrow agent will be instructed not to disburse any funds until the
following conditions are met:

(a) Satisfactory title insurance coverage will be obtained for all ioans, with the title insurance
policy naming the Company as the insured and providing title insurance in an amount equal to the
principal amount of the loan. Title insurance insures only the validity and priority of the Company’s deed
of trust, and does not insure the Company against loss by reason of other causes, such as diminution in the
value of the security property, over-appraisals, borrower’s defaults, etc.

(b) Satisfactory fire and casualty insurance has been obtained for all loans, or only casualty
insurance in the event of a Loan secured by unimproved land, which insurance shall name the Company
as loss payee in an amount equal to the principal amount of the Company’s loan. (See “VII. Risk Factors
~ Uninsured Losses,”)

(c) The Manager does not intend to arrange for mortgage insurance, which would afford
some protection against loss if the Company foreclosed on a loan and there were insufficient equity in the
security property to repay all sums owed.

(d) All loan documents (notes, deeds of trust, etc.) and insurance policies will name the
Company as payee and beneficiary or additional loss insured, as applicable. In the event the Company
purchases loans, the Company shall receive assignments of all beneficial interest in any documents
related to each Loan so purchased. Company investments in Loans will not be held in the name of the
Manager or any other nominee.

Sale of Loans Generally

The Company will make mortgage loans for investment and does not expect to engage in real estate
operations in the ordinary course of business {except as may be required if the Company forecloses on a

property). The Company may also sell non-performing Portfolio Loans or foreclosed property securing

loans or enter into inter-creditor agreements when the Manager determines that it appears to be
advantageous for the Company to do so, based upon then current interest rates, the length of time that the
loan has been held by the Company, and the overall investment objectives of the Company.

Leveraging the Portfolio

third party lender. This “spread” between the interest eared on a leveraged loan and the interest paid on

1732	Under the non-contingent bond method, the issuer of a contingent debt instrument must first determine
1733	the Comparable Yield. The Comparable Yield is the yield at which the Company could issue a debt
1734	instrument with terms and conditions similar to those of the contingent payment debt instrument. The
1735	Company has selected 8% as its Comparable Yield, and this rate will be used by the Company for
1736	purposes of determining its own taxable income and for any required information reporting. Since there
1737	is no direct authority in this area, it is uncertain whether the Internal Revenue Service will agree with this
1738	determination and may require a higher or lower Comparative Yield. If the Internal Revenue Service
1739	determines that the Comparable Yield should be higher, a Noteholder will be required to accrue the
1740	difference between the Comparable Yield selected by the Company and such higher Yield as additional
1741	interest income earned each year, even though there are no payments of contingent interest in such year.

1759	
1760	If a Note is sold, redeemed or otherwise disposed of, the selling Noteholder will recognize gain or loss
1761	equal to the difference between the amount realized from the disposition and the selling Noteholder's
1762	adjusted basis in such Note. The adjusted basis generally will equal the cost of such Note to the seller,
1763	increased by any original issue discount on such Note included in the seller's income and reduced (but not
1764	below zero) by any non-contingent payments on the Note. Because the Notes are characterized as
1765	contingent debt instruments under the Treasury Regulations, any gain recognized upon a sale, exchange,
1766	retirement, or other disposition of a Note will generally be ordinary income and any loss will be ordinary
1767	to the extent of prior ordinary income inclusion.

rules that differ significantly from those summarized below. This summary applies only to “U.S. Holders”

prospective investor is urged to consult its tax advisor regarding the U.S. federal, state, local, and foreign
income and other tax considerations relating to an investment in the Notes.

For this purpose, a “U.S. Holder” is a beneficial owner of the Notes that is, for U.S. federal income tax
purposes, (i) an individual who is a citizen or resident of the United States, (ii) a corporation, or other

of which is subject to the primary supervision of a United States court and which has one or more United

Original Issue Discount

The Company may be deemed for tax purposes to pay to the holders of Notes “additional interest”, as
such concept is described in the following discussion, Consequently, the Company will treat the Notes as
contingent debt instruments subject to the "non-contingent bond method" of reporting interest as set forth
in applicable Treasury Regulations. As a result of the classification of the Notes as contingent debt
instruments, any gain realized on the sale or exchange of the Notes may be treated as ordinary income, in
whole or in part. See “Gain or Loss on Disposition".

Under the non-contingent bond method, the issuer of a contingent debt instrument must first determine
the Comparable Yield. The Comparable Yield is the yield at which the Company could issue a debt
instrument with terms and conditions similar to those of the contingent payment debt instrument. The
Company has selected 8% as its Comparable Yield, and this rate will be used by the Company for
purposes of determining its own taxable income and for any required information reporting. Since there
is no direct authority in this area, it is uncertain whether the Internal Revenue Service will agree with this
determination and may require a higher or lower Comparative Yield. If the Internal Revenue Service
determines that the Comparable Yield should be higher, a Noteholder will be required to accrue the
difference between the Comparable Yield selected by the Company and such higher Yield as additional
interest income earned each year, even though there are no payments of contingent interest in such year.

Under the non-contingent bond method, if the interest payable for any period is greater or less than the
amount projected, the amount of income included for that period would be either increased or decreased
accordingly. Any net increase in the projected contingent payments for a taxable year (e.g., a
determination of the amount due pursuant to the additional interest) is treated by a holder as additional
interest income.

Please note that the Comparable Yield is supplied by the Company solely for computing income under
the non-contingent bond method for federal income tax purposes, and does not constitute a projection or
representation as to the amounts that Noteholders will actually receive with respect to their Notes.

Gain or Loss on Disposition

If a Note is sold, redeemed or otherwise disposed of, the selling Noteholder will recognize gain or loss
equal to the difference between the amount realized from the disposition and the selling Noteholder's
adjusted basis in such Note. The adjusted basis generally will equal the cost of such Note to the seller,
increased by any original issue discount on such Note included in the seller's income and reduced (but not
below zero) by any non-contingent payments on the Note. Because the Notes are characterized as
contingent debt instruments under the Treasury Regulations, any gain recognized upon a sale, exchange,
retirement, or other disposition of a Note will generally be ordinary income and any loss will be ordinary
to the extent of prior ordinary income inclusion.

exempt entities generally is exempt from federal income taxation, except to the extent of “unrelated
business taxable income” (UBT) in excess of $1,000 in any year.

ERISA CONSIDERATIONS

If you are the fiduciary of an Employee benefit plan (“Plan Investor’) subject to the Employee
Retirement Income Security Act of 1974, as amended (“ERISA”), or section 4975 of the Internal
Revenue Code of 1986, as amended (the “Cede”), you are urged to consult with your own counsel
regarding the application of ERISA and the Code to your purchase. The following is intended to be a
summary only and is not a substitute for careful planning with a professional.

Fiduciary Considerations

In considering a purchase of the Notes, fiduciaries of Plan Investors should consider their basic fiduciary
duty under ERISA that requires them to discharge their investment duties prudently and solely in the
interest of plan participants and beneficiaries. In making such a determination, a fiduciary of a Plan
Investor should be sure that the investment is in accordance with the governing instruments and the
overall policies of the plan, and that the investment will comply with the diversification and prudence
requirements of ERISA. Plan Investor fiduciaries should consider the role that a purchase of the Notes
would play in the plan’s overail investment portfolio.

In addition, provisions of ERISA and the Code prohibit transactions involving the assets of a plan and
persons who have specified relationships with a plan (“Parties in Interest” under ERISA and “Disqualified
Persons” under the Cade, collectively referred to herein as “Parties in Interesf’), unless an exemption is
available for such transaction. A Plan Investor fiduciary should be sure that purchase of Notes will not
constitute or give rise to a direct or indirect non-exempt prohibited transaction. In particular, Plan
Investors must make an independent investment decision with respect to their purchase of Notes issued by
the Company and must not rely upon the Manager or its affiliates for investment advice regarding such
participation.

a

ERISA and its accompanying regulations are complex and, to a great extent, have not yet been interpreted
by the courts or the administrative agencies. This discussion only addresses certain features of ERISA as
it applies to the Notes, and does not purport to constitute a thorough analysis of ERISA with respect to
your investment in the Company.

EACH INVESTOR SUBJECT TO ERISA SHOULD CONSULT WITH
ITS OWN LEGAL COUNSEL CONCERNING THE IMPLICATIONS
UNDER ERISA OF THE OWNERSHIP OF NOTES.

CERTAIN OTHER REGULATORY CONSIDERATIONS

The operation of the Company and the ownership of the Notes by Noteholders will be structured so as not
to subject the Fund to the provisions of the Investment Company Act of 1940 (the “Znvestment Company
Acf’). In the alternative, the Company expects to rely, among other things, on the exemption from
registration afforded by compliance with Section 3(c)(5) of the Investment Company Act. Section 3(c)(5)
excludes from the definition of “investment company” issuers of non-redeemable securities engaged in
“purchasing or otherwise acquiring mortgages and other liens on and interests in real estate”.

The Notes are being issued without registration under the Securities Act of 1933 (the “Securities Act’) by
reason of the exemptions from the registration requirements for private offerings set forth in Section 4(2)
and Rule 506 of Regulation D of the Securities Act. As such, the Notes cannot be resold except pursuant
to registration under the Securities Act or an exemption therefrom.

In addition, the Notes are being issued pursuant to exemptions or permits under applicable state securities
laws, and cannot be resold except in compliance with restrictions imposed by such laws.

CONSIDERATIONS RELATING TO STATUS OF
NOTEHOLDERS AND COMPANY AS LENDERS

The Company is a lender with respect to its Portfolio Loans, and, for certain purposes, the Company may
be deemed a borrower and the Noteholders may be deemed lenders with respect to the Notes. California
and other states have numerous laws and regulations which apply to the activities of lenders and the rights
of borrowers. The applicability of these laws and regulations, and their exemptions and exclusions, are
frequently complex and highly fact-specific, and they vary by jurisdiction and are subject to change. In
addition, litigation in a number of states has imposed liability upon lenders, or otherwise adversely
impacted lenders, in ways to which Noteholders may not be accustomed as a result of other investment
activities.

Usury

A number of states have adopted usury laws, which generally prohibit the charging of interest in certain
circumstances in excess of a statutorily-defined rate. The rates of interest to be paid to the Noteholders by
the Company, and the rates of interest to be paid by the Company’s Portfolio Borrowers to the Company,
may exceed the applicable statutorily-defined usury rates. As of November 2007, charging interest at a
rate greater than ten percent (10%) per annum is usurious in California unless an exemption or exclusion
therefrom exists, but such threshold rate may change in the future in California or rates in other
jurisdictions may be applicable. As a result, were any of the capital loans made by the Noteholders to the
Company or by the Company to the Portfolio Borrowers to be challenged, as usurious, in certain
circumstances, such as in a bankruptcy, it is possible other creditors, a bankruptcy trustee or receiver or
another interested party (an “Interested Party”) would be able to successfully invalidate all or a portion of
the interest due to the Noteholders or to the Company. This could result in a court imposing treble
damages or other penalties and fines, including criminal penalties.

The Company intends to rely on qualified advisors and use commercially reasonable efforts to comply
with laws and regulations applying to lenders and borrowers, and to seek exemptions and exclusions as
advisable from such laws where appropriate to meet the investment objectives of the Company and this
offering,

Lending Laws

The California Finance Lenders Law and similar statues in other states may permit a borrower or a person
acting on behalf of a borrower to avoid paying principal and interest on any loan made by a person
required to be licensed under such a statute who does not become so registered. Any Noteholder that is
not properly licensed as a finance lender in a jurisdiction which requires such licensing in connection with
its loans to the Company may risk having its ability to collect principal and interest from the Company
challenged by an Interested Party in any adversarial proceeding relating to the Company, such as
bankruptcy. In addition, the Company itself may be subject to such risk in connection with its Loans to
the Portfolio Borrowers.

The Company expects to make its Portfolio Loans pursuant to a finance lender’s license issued by
California and other jurisdictions as applicable. The Company also intends to rely on qualified advisors
and use commercially reasonable efforts to comply with laws and regulations applying to lenders and
borrowers, and to seek exemptions and exclusions as advisable from such laws where appropriate to meet
the investment objectives of the Company and this offering. The Manager anticipates that such efforts

Lender Liability

As an additional consideration, legal decisions in many jurisdictions, including California, have imposed
liability upon lenders for actions such as declaring defaults with respect to loans and refusing to meet
Company loan commitments under certain circumstances. In addition, some courts have permitted
litigants to pursue claims against lenders for environmental torts of a borrower and other liability as a
result of their association with a borrower. Such so-called “lender liability” is a developing and uncertain
area of the law, and there can be no assurance that such a claim could not be brought against the
